Lech Lecha.title: Abraham Was a Soul Winner

blocks.t: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” (Gen 12:4–5)

It literally says in the Hebrew text that Abraham and Sarah took “the souls that they had won in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” Abraham was a soul winner. It is written, “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise.” (Pr 11:30 NKJV)

Later on, when Abraham went to war against the kings who had taken Lot captive, it says, “he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan.” (Ge 14:14) In the traditional, English Jewish Chumash translation it says, “he armed his disciples who had been born in his house—three hundred and eighteen of them—and he pursued them as far as Dan.”

The calling to be a father and mother is not limited to having your own children. It also includes becoming parents to spiritual children by making disciples. That is what Abraham and Sarah did. God needs many such “fathers and mothers in Israel” in our time. Abraham and Sarah did not have many children of their own, but they had many disciples. They were known for their hospitality, which is described later on, in chapter 18. They invited guests and strangers into their tents, gave them delicious food and taught them about the only true God. This was how they “won souls.”

It is written, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.” (Heb 13:2) We know that this happened to Abraham and Sarah. (See Genesis 18.) Our homes are so important. The first believers all met in homes. They are to be houses of worship, the best environment for making disciples, training them to obey God’s commandments and walk in God’s ways. It says of Abraham, “Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” (Ge 26:5) He taught his disciples to also follow these commandments.

One Jewish tradition, which should be taken with a grain of salt, says that Abraham gave all of his guests the very best food possible. While they ate together, he taught them about the only true God. If they refused to join him in giving thanks to God after they had eaten, he forced them to pay for their food.

The expressions “sons” and “disciples” are used synonymously in the Scriptures, and also in Jewish tradition. Disciples are called “sons” or “children.” This is probably how the text in Acts should be understood when it says, “Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.” (Ac 19:14) Most likely, it is referring to seven disciples of this Jewish priest, who went around trying to cast out demons. Yeshua said to his disciples, “Little children, yet a little while I am with you.” (Jn 13:33) Both Paul and John used the same expression for their disciples. (See 1 Co 4:14, Gal 4:19, 1 Jn 2:1, and 3 Jn v.4.)

A Master and his disciples make up a “family,” or as it is also expressed, “a house.” The disciples of the most famous rabbis in the second Temple period, Hillel and Shammai, were called “the house of Hillel” and “the house of Shammai.” It says in Hebrews, “Messiah is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.” (Heb 3:6) We are disciples who belong to “the house of Messiah.” He is our Master.

The Great Commission involves much more than getting people to pray a prayer of salvation. It is all about making disciples, who learn to keep God’s commandments. “And Yeshua came and said to them, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.’” (Mt 28:18–20)

Making disciples is a time-consuming enterprise that requires a lot of hard work. It is just like raising children. It takes time, much effort and much prayer. But this is what we have been commanded to do. We should get as many children of our own as possible, but we should also make many disciples. Our own children are our primary and most important disciples. It must begin with them, as it is written, “All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children.” (Isa 54:13)

It is never too late to begin making disciples. On the contrary, the older we get the more wisdom we have to give others. One of the rabbis in the time of Yeshua said, “Be scrupulous in your tithing and make many disciples!” These are good rules to follow. Abraham and Sarah did both. They tithed (Gen 14:20), and they had many disciples (Gen 14:14).

Vayera.title: The Binding of Isaac

blocks.t: “After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, ‘Abraham!’ And he said, ‘Here am I.’ He said, ‘Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you.’” (Gen 22:1–2)

This was the tenth and final test that Abraham, the father of all who believe, had to go through—and it was the most difficult of them all. It was the very climax in his walk of faith. God’s command seemed to be beyond all reason. Finally, the promised son had been born. Should Abraham now sacrifice his beloved son, whom he loved so much? Isaac meant everything to Abraham.

We can compare this test with Yeshua’s words to his disciples, after they had recognized him to be the long-awaited Messiah. He then told them that he must be killed and on the third day be raised again. What was Peter’s response? “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” (Mt 16:22)

It is not difficult to see a parallel between the text in verse 2, ‘Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,…and offer him’ and John 3:16. Many Jews read Genesis 22 every time before they pray their morning prayers. It is one of the most frequently read chapters in the entire Bible among the Jewish people, the very foundation of Israel’s relationship with God.

Abraham did not hesitate. He knew that it was God who had spoken to him and he had learnt to trust Him, so he obeyed since he had a covenant with God. The next verse says, “So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him.” (v. 3)

Notice that God had told him about a special place. The following verse gives us another insight into why Abraham obeyed. It reads, “On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.” (v. 4) What did Abraham see when he lifted up his eyes? It says that he saw “the place”. “The place” is in Hebrew ha-makom (הַמָּקוֹם). It is mentioned three times in this chapter, in verses 3, 4 and 9. Ha-makom is an important word in the Scriptures, used about the place where God dwells and reveals Himself.

Abraham saw “the place” from afar on the third day. “The third day” in the Scriptures always refers to the resurrection. Yeshua explained this to his disciples after his resurrection. “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and said to them, ‘Thus it is written, that the Messiah should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead.” (Lk 24:45–46) According to Yeshua, this is the summary of all the Scriptures.
The Book of Hebrews confirms to us what Abraham saw,

“By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.’ He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” (Heb 11:17–19)

When Abraham lifted his eyes on the third day, he saw in the distance Golgotha and the resurrection of the Messiah two thousand years in advance! Further on in the story, Abraham told Isaac, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” (v. 8)
“And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.” (v. 6)

It is important to note in the text, not only Abraham’s obedience, but also Isaac’s complete obedience and surrender to his father. This is repeated again in verse 8, “So they went both of them together.” Isaac was at this time at least 30 years old. He was probably just as old as the Messiah was when he prayed in the garden, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” (Mt 26:39)

The Hebrew root word for “the wood” that Abraham placed on Isaac is the same as the one used about the cross that Yeshua carried on his back. “…and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called the place of a skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.” (Jn 19:17)
“When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.” (v. 9)

Among the Jewish people, this whole passage is called “the binding of Isaac” or just “the binding.” The Hebrew word that is used is akedah (עֲקֵדָה). This is the only time that this form of the word occurs in the Scriptures. According to Rashi, the word means that the hands and feet of Isaac were tied behind his back and they were tied so hard that it left marks on Isaac’s hands and feet. It is obvious that the old man Abraham could not have done this to Isaac without his consent. He submitted to his father all the way unto death. The binding of Isaac was a unique event pointing forward to the most unique event in human history: the sacrifice of Messiah at Golgotha!

Chayei Sarah.title: Sarah’s Death

blocks.t: “Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.” (Gen 23:1-2)

Yeshua said, “For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.” (Matt 11:13) This does not mean that everything in the Torah was fulfilled by the time John came, but it means that the Torah and the prophets began to be fulfilled at that time. The Torah still prophesies. It will do so as long as heaven and earth exist (Mt 5:17-18 and Lk 16:16-17). It is written in the book of Hebrews “…the law has a shadow of the good things to come.” (Heb 10:1, revised translation). Not everything in the Torah has been fulfilled yet.
This week’s Torah portion is about two women—Sarah and Rebekah. We are going to take a look at the prophetic spiritual truths revealed in the lives of these two women.

The previous chapter ended with the account of the binding of Isaac, and this portion begins by speaking about Sarah’s death. Jewish tradition holds that Sarah died from the shock of hearing that Abraham had gone to sacrifice Isaac. In any case, Abraham was not there when she died, for it says that he came to mourn for her.

There is a deeper prophetic meaning behind this connection between Sarah’s death and the binding of Isaac. As we have mentioned before, Sarah is a prophetic type of God’s heavenly design for Jerusalem. Paul wrote,

“Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise. Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, ‘Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.’ Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.” (Gal 4:22–28)

Just as Isaac was the son of Sarah, so all those who belong to Messiah are figuratively the sons of Sarah, according to Paul. It is written about Jerusalem in Psalm 87:5–7, “And of Zion it shall be said, ‘This one and that one were born in her; for the Most High himself will establish her. The Lord records as he registers the peoples; This one was born there.’ Selah. Singers and dancers alike say, ‘All my springs are in you.’”

Galatians 4:27 quotes from Isaiah 54:1. That entire chapter is speaking of the future restoration of Jerusalem. It says in verses 11–12, “O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones.” God will one day transform the present earthly Jerusalem. We can compare what is written in Isaiah 54 with the heavenly Jerusalem that John describes in the book of Revelation.

“…its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal. It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed…The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel.” (Rev 21:11–12, 18–19)

It is important to understand that the heavenly Jerusalem described in the Book of Revelation is talking about a restored Jerusalem here on the earth. The first followers of the Messiah, Jews and Gentiles alike, all had this understanding. Their hope for the future was connected to the restoration of Jerusalem. The early church father, Justin Martyr, wrote about this in his book Dialogue with Trypho the Jew in the middle of the second century. In the book, the Rabbi Trypho at one point asks Justin,

“Do you admit as the truth, that this place Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and do you expect that your people will be regathered and rejoice with Christ, together with the patriarchs and the prophets and the saints among our people, and even those who have become proselytes before Christ came…?”

[Justin’s answer:] “I have confirmed to you before, that I and many others really hold this to be true, just as you yourself well know this …I and all other completely orthodox Christians, know that there will be a resurrection in the flesh and also a thousand years in Jerusalem, rebuilt, adorned and enlarged, as the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah, and all of the other prophets say. And furthermore, a man among us called John, one of the apostles of Christ, prophesied in a Revelation given to him that those who had believed in our Christ, will be allowed to live in Jerusalem for a thousand years and after that the universal, that is the eternal resurrection for all will happen and also the judgment.”

According to Justin Martyr, the heavenly Jerusalem of the Book of Revelation is the same city that Ezekiel, Isaiah and others described as a restored, earthly Jerusalem. All “orthodox Christians” during the second century had the exact same hope for the future as all Jews have had throughout history. It took at least three centuries for this biblical hope to disappear. Sarah is a picture of the restored, heavenly Jerusalem described by the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah, and even John in the book of Revelation.

The binding of Isaac is a picture of the death and resurrection of Messiah. Just as the death of Sarah is mentioned in connection with the binding of Isaac, so Jerusalem was destroyed shortly after the death and resurrection of Yeshua. The glory vanished. Jerusalem was trampled underfoot by Gentiles and the long exile began. However, before the mention of Sarah’s death, the Torah tells of one important detail: the birth of Rebekah!

“Now after these things it was told to Abraham, ‘Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel. Bethuel fathered Rebekah.’” (Gen 22:20-23)
We will look closer at this prophetic picture later.

Toldot.title: The Birth Right

blocks.t: “Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted. And Esau said to Jacob, ‘Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!’ (Therefore his name was called Edom.) Jacob said, ‘Sell me your birthright now.’ Esau said, ‘I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?’ Jacob said, ‘Swear to me now.’ So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.” (Gen 25:29-34)

Why did Jacob buy the birthright from Esau? The view most people have is that Jacob was selfish and deceitful. There is, however, another, more Scriptural side to this. Remember that Jacob had been listening to the teaching and wisdom of Abraham and had heard about the promises and the calling that God had given to his descendants. Esau, on the other hand, showed no interest in this tremendous spiritual inheritance. It was the calling and the promises given to Abraham that mattered most to Jacob.

Would the right of the firstborn, to this enormous spiritual calling to be the heir of the whole world, be given to a person that neither showed any interest in them, nor seemed to be spiritually qualified? Rebekah had most likely also told Jacob which of the two God had chosen. The pot of stew was Jacob’s test to find out how much the calling meant to Esau. Esau considered the satisfaction of his hunger to be of greater importance than God’s eternal calling.

From this story, the Book of Hebrews warns us—not about what Jacob did, but about what Esau did. It does not say, “See to it that you do not act like Jacob.” It says rather, “See to it …that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.” (Heb 12:15-16) Jacob fought his whole life for the birthright. Esau despised it. The Torah says of Esau, “he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.” (v. 34) Esau’s example is a warning against being someone who primarily lives for selfish pleasures and carnal desires.

In the next chapter of the Torah, it says that Esau chose to marry two Canaanite women. “When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.” (Gen 26:34-35) This demonstrates how ignorant Esau was about spiritual matters, and how little he valued them. He was also very selfish and insensitive, since he did not realize how grievous his behavior was to Isaac and Rebekah until many years later, when Isaac blessed Jacob and sent him away to get a bride from Abraham’s relatives.

“Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, ‘You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women,’ and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father, Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebaioth.” (Gen 28:6-9)

Esau, however, never repented. He simply added one more wife to his harem. The unholy and sexually immoral son of Isaac married the daughter of the unholy and sexually immoral son of Abraham. This marriage only made the situation worse, but Esau did not understand this. He was completely ignorant of spiritual things.

Vayetze.title: God’s Unshakable Promise to Jacob

blocks.t: “And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, ‘I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.’” (Gen 28:13–15)

Here, we see God’s irrevocable promise to the descendants of Jacob. “Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” (v. 15) For two thousand years, God has kept His people during their long exile to the ends of the earth; and in our day, He has begun to bring them back again to their Land, just as He promised Jacob. This is a unique, unparalleled phenomenon in the history of mankind. Truly, YHWH is the shepherd of Israel. “Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, ‘He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.’” (Jer 31:10)

God’s promise to all of Jacob’s descendants stands firm, “The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” (v. 13–14)

Peter explained to the Jews who had gathered for afternoon prayer in the Temple, “You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.” (Acts 3:25–26)

Jacob inherited the promise made to Abraham, “in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” (v. 14) Not one dot in the Torah shall disappear, as long as heaven and earth exist. Every part of the promise God gave to Jacob and his descendants will be fulfilled. “The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring.…I…will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” (v. 13, 15)

The place where Jacob slept and dreamed is located within the area where the politicians of the world who are in line with the “Two State Solution” want to establish a Palestinian state. There is a battle today for this small piece of land, and it involves the entire world. The leaders in Jerusalem two thousand years ago chose to kill Yeshua and instead released a murderer. Similarly, the leaders of the nations today want to release a nation of terrorists and thereby sacrifice the Jewish state, since the prospective remaining area of the Promised Land would be impossible to defend.

We have to remember that it is the credibility of the Creator of the universe that is at stake here. He is the one who has made the promise. He cannot lie and He cannot go back on His word. His promise will be fulfilled. “I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” Paul wrote about this election of Jacob, “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of his call— she was told, ‘The older will serve the younger.’ As it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’” (Ro 9:11–13)

The exact same promise given to Abraham was repeated to Jacob, “in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” Concerning Abraham, Paul wrote that the “offspring” is a reference to Messiah. Isaac, who was born supernaturally through the power of the promise, is a picture of this. However, at Bethel, the Eternal says that through the descendants of Jacob, the twelve tribes of Israel, all the families of the world will be blessed. Jacob’s twelve sons were all born in natural ways. Before Jacob left the Promised Land, God promised him that his descendants would become a blessing to all the nations of the world. In the same way, Paul also wrote, “For I tell you that Messiah became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs.” (Ro 15:8) Messiah did not come to take away the promises from the Jewish people, but to confirm them.

The promise that the descendants of Jacob would bless all the families of the earth has also been fulfilled already, in many different ways. The Holy Scriptures have been given to the world through this people. Messiah came, according to the flesh, from Israel. The Gospel has come to the nations from this people, and so on. In our day, we can also see that many of the Nobel prizes are given to the Jewish people. Ninety percent of all the seeds of the vegetables eaten in Europe come from the tiny nation of Israel, and the list of contributions goes on. And just like the Messiah came the first time through the Jewish people, He will also return to the Jewish people and bless the world with life from the dead.

Vayishlach.title: Jacob Wrestles with God

blocks.t: “And Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with him. Then he said, ‘Let me go, for the day has broken.’ But Jacob said, ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ And he said to him, ‘What is your name?’ And he said, ‘Jacob.’ Then he said, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.’ Then Jacob asked him, ‘Please tell me your name.’ But he said, ‘Why is it that you ask my name?’ And there he blessed him. So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, ‘For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.’” (Gen 32:24–30)

God’s promises can sometimes only be fulfilled through an intense battle in prayer. Jacob is the foremost example we have in the Scriptures of this. He never gave up, and in the end he was victorious. Jacob loved the things of God and His blessings. He loved to sit by the tents and listen to the Word of God. He longed for the right of the firstborn and the blessing of Abraham, and in the end he received both.

“In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God. He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us— the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is his memorial name.” (Hos 12:3–5)

In Jacob’s own words, he met God face to face during the wrestling in the night at Peniel. Notice also that Hosea connected this incident with Jacob’s return to Bethel. (More about this later.) When the angel told Jacob to let go, Jacob instead cried out with tears, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

David said about Jacob, “This is Jacob, the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face. Selah” (Ps 24:6 NKJV) The angel answered Jacob, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.” (v. 28) May we be like Jacob, who sought God with such intensity, so that we also can become Israel—ones who overcome! We need to learn to fight in prayer with God like Jacob did.

Jacob did not know whom he fought with. “Then Jacob asked him, ‘Please tell me your name.’ But he said, ‘Why is it that you ask my name?’ And there he blessed him. So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, ‘For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.’” (Gen 32:29–30) First, it says that it was a man. “And a man wrestled with him” (v. 24). Afterwards, however, Jacob said, “I have seen God face to face,” (v. 30) and Hosea says that it was an angel. “He strove with the angel.” (Hos 12:4)

In Scripture, there is only one person that is both called “man” and “angel,” as well as “God,” and that is Messiah. Prophetically, Jacob’s meeting with God at Peniel is a picture of the Jewish people’s encounter with Messiah in the end times, “And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication. They will look on me, the one they have pierced.” (Zec 12:10) This is God’s preordained solution to the conflict in the Middle East, as it says in the next verse, “The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel.” (v. 31)

When Jacob’s descendants in the end times have an encounter with God through Messiah, a glorious new day will begin for the whole world and the Messianic kingdom will begin. It is written in Malachi, “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings.” (Mal 4:2) David prophesied about the Messiah, “The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth.” (2 Sa 23:3–4)

The angel promised Jacob that his name would be changed to Israel. A name change is, in Scripture, a picture of a new birth. The name change, however, was not completely fulfilled until later on at Bethel, as we will see.

“God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him. And God said to him, ‘Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.’ So he called his name Israel.” (Gen 35:9–10)

Vayishlach.book: Messiah in the Torah, Vol. I

Vayeshev.title: Joseph Is Rejected by His Brothers

blocks.t: “Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors. But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.” (Gen 37:3–4)

Joseph was Rachel’s firstborn. It says that Israel loved Joseph more than the other brothers because he was the son of his old age. Benjamin was, however, even younger, born eight years after Joseph. According to Rashi, Jacob had, however, already developed a special affection for Joseph during those years. A Jewish Midrash interprets the phrase “because he was the son of his old age” to mean that Joseph resembled Jacob in his face. It says in the Book of Ecclesiastes, “Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man’s wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.” (Ecc 8:1) The idea that Joseph resembled Jacob in his face suggests that Joseph had inherited Jacob’s spiritual wisdom and prophetic insight. He was the anointed rightful heir among Jacob’s twelve sons.

Jacob gave Joseph “a robe of many colors.” This means that Jacob gave Joseph the position of firstborn among the brothers as their leader. The robe also symbolized his messianic calling as king of Israel. Paul wrote of Messiah, “He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.” (Col 1:18)

Note also that the Torah states that it was Israel who loved Joseph more than the rest of his sons, and who gave him the special robe. “Israel” is the name the Torah uses about Jacob’s transformed, heavenly nature. This shows us that the choice of Joseph above the others was not only because of Jacob’s personal preferences or affections, but because of a prophetic act of God. Joseph was the one God had chosen among the brothers, and Jacob knew it. This, however, caused the other brothers to hate Joseph. Just as the nations hate the nation of Israel because they are chosen, the brothers similarly hated Joseph because he was chosen. It says that they could not even speak kindly to him. John wrote about Yeshua, “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him in the end.” (Jn 1:11) The Torah later on describes how Joseph’s brothers received him. Israel will also one day receive Yeshua. What a day that will be!

Joseph went on to tell his brothers about dreams that he had. In the Torah, dreams convey prophetic messages. Joseph was in other words also a prophet, just as it is also written about Yeshua (see Mt 21:11 and Lk 24:19). When Joseph told them his dreams, they hated him even more and also began to envy him. Envy is even more dangerous than hatred. It was envy that caused the first murder, and envy was also a reason behind Yeshua’s death sentence. It is written about Pilate, “For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.” (Mk 15:10)

“Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, ‘Hear this dream that I have dreamed: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf.’ His brothers said to him, ‘Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?’ So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.” (v. 5–8)

“His brothers said to him, ‘Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?’” (v. 8) Reigning is done by consent. Ruling is done with force. The brothers ruled out both options. The dream had to do with sheaves of grain, symbolizing bread, which is necessary for survival. This dream was fulfilled in Egypt, when the brothers came there to buy grain in order to survive.

“Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, ‘Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.’ But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, ‘What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?’ And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.” (v. 9–11)

The second dream—about the sun, the moon, and the stars—was a Messianic prophecy about the resurrection and the world to come, since it also included his mother Rachel, who was already dead. Scripture compares our resurrected bodies with the heavenly bodies.

“And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.” (Dan 12:2–3)
“Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” (Mt 13:43)

“There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So is it with the resurrection of the dead.” (1 Co 15:40–42)

Jacob openly rebuked Joseph for this dream, but he took it to heart. Jacob was most likely trying to calm the brothers’ hatred and envy toward Joseph. But to himself, he probably took it as a confirmation of the choice he had made. The dream is also an indication of Messiah’s divinity, because a father and mother would otherwise never bow before their own son. Joseph was something more than just their son.

Miketz.title: Joseph Is Exalted

blocks.t: “Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, ‘Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are. You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you.’ And Pharaoh said to Joseph, ‘See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.’ Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen and put a gold chain about his neck. And he made him ride in his second chariot. And they called out before him, ‘Bow the knee!’ Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.” (Gen 41:39–43)

Pharaoh had all power and authority over Egypt. In this, Pharaoh is a picture of Almighty God and Joseph a picture of the exaltation of Messiah after His resurrection to sit on the Father’s right hand. “And they called out before him, ‘Bow the knee!’ Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.” (v. 43) It is written about Yeshua:

“Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Yeshua every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Yeshua the Messiah is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Php 2:9–11)
“And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. So Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.” (v. 45)

In order to rule over the anti-Semitic Egypt, Joseph needed a new Egyptian name. Pharaoh therefore changed Joseph’s name to Zaphenath-paneah, which, according to Rashi and Rashbam, means “He who unveils secrets.” This is a picture of how Yeshua, after His resurrection, became known among the Gentiles by His Greek name “Iesous,” which later on became “Jesus,” in English. The name “Jesus” is completely detached from His Jewish or Hebrew identity, just like Joseph’s new name Zaphenath-paneah was. We also see in the text a foreshadowing of how His gospel has spread across the nations, as it says, “So Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.”

When the old righteous man Simeon took Yeshua up in his arms after He was born, he said, “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” (Lk 2:29–32) Just as the light of the gospel has spread out over the nations among the Gentiles, so Yeshua also will soon become the glory of Israel.

Pharaoh gave Joseph in marriage to “Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On.” According to the sages, Potiphera is the same person as Potiphar. He is called a priest in this passage, which is not so strange since it was common in those days that people in authority were also called priests. Joseph was faithful to God and lived a pure life. Instead of a few moments of sinful pleasure with Potiphar’s wife, he therefore received his daughter as a wife. “Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.” (Jas 1:12) Pharaoh did this also in order to exonerate Joseph from the false accusations that had led to his imprisonment.

“Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore them to him. Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh. ‘For,’ he said, ‘God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.’ The name of the second he called Ephraim, ‘For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.’” (v. 50–52)

The Torah mentions twice that the sons were born to Joseph. Even though Joseph had an Egyptian wife, who was also the daughter of a priest, she bore the sons to Joseph. The Torah emphasizes that the sons did not assimilate and become Egyptians. They are prophetic types of the Gentiles who have come to faith in Yeshua, Messiah ben Joseph, and become His disciples. Disciples are also called “children,” in the Scriptures. The name of the first son was “Manasseh.” His name comes from the Hebrew word nashah (נָשָׁה), which means “to forget.” Joseph said, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”

Manasseh, in particular, is a picture of the first generation of Gentiles who became followers of Messiah and were grafted into Israel, but later forgot their connection to the Jewish people. Joseph’s second son, Ephraim, is a picture of the Gentile followers of Messiah in the last generation, who will understand that they have been grafted into Israel, and will reconnect with the Jewish people and where Jerusalem once again will be at the center, see Ro 15:25–27.

“Ephraim” is a double form of the Hebrew word ephrathah (אֶפְרָתָה), which means “fruitful.” Ephraim can be translated “doubly fruitful.” The last harvest among the Gentiles will be even greater than the first. Joseph said, “For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” Even though Joseph had become ruler over all of Egypt, he still called Egypt “the land of my affliction.” Joseph belonged in Israel, and still longed for his Land. In the same way, Messiah is waiting eagerly for the day when He will return to Jerusalem. “…whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago.” (Ac 3:21) “This Yeshua, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” (Ac 1:11)

To this day, Jewish fathers bless their sons every Shabbat by saying, “May God bless you and make you like Ephraim and Manasseh!” This is a prayer that the sons, like Ephraim and Manasseh, will be fruitful and multiply, and not become assimilated during the time of Israel’s exile. But it is also indirectly and unknowingly a prayer that they will become disciples and followers of Mashiach ben Yoseph. We know who He is, and this prayer will one day be answered!

Beresheet.title: The Messiah Is the Beginning

blocks.t: The Messiah is the goal that the Torah points towards. The first word in the Torah is Beresheet (בְּרֵאשִׁית) in Hebrew, which is translated as “In the beginning.” Resheet means “beginning.” Be is a prefix that is usually translated as “in,” “through” or “of.” “The beginning” is one of the titles of the Messiah. He says, “Behold, I am coming soon,… I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” (Rev 22:12–13) The first verse in the Torah can therefore be translated: “Through the Beginning [Messiah], God created the heavens and the earth.” This is what the Apostles tell us, as well.

“For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together. … He is the beginning.” (Col 1:16–18)

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (Jn 1:1–3)

Just as the Messiah is the beginning of all things, He is also the end. Paul writes, “making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Messiah as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.” (Eph 1:9–10)

Therefore, the Scriptures do not only begin with Messiah, they also end with Him. The last verses in the Bible read, “He who testifies to these things says, ‘Surely I am coming soon.’ Amen. Come, Lord Yeshua! The grace of the Lord Yeshua be with all. Amen.” (Rev 22:20– 21) The Messiah is the first and the last, the beginning and the end. All things begin with Him and end with Him. He is the main message of the Torah and all of Scripture. Yeshua said, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.” (Jn 5:46) And Paul wrote, “For the goal at which the Torah aims is the Messiah.” (Ro 10:4 Complete Jewish Bible)

The Messiah is the Word through which the worlds came into being. He was revealed two thousand years ago when He became a man in Yeshua of Nazareth. The Apostle John writes, “The true light, which enlightens everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.” (Jn 1:9–10)
The Scriptures are a progressive revelation about God. This means two important things:
1. The revelation grows throughout the Scriptures;
2. Later revelation never abolishes, but always builds on earlier revelation.

This can be compared to the light that comes from a spotlight. It has an origin in one point. From that point, the beam of light becomes wider and wider. The Scriptures begin in the first verse with the Messiah. He is the Beginning. Everything comes from Him. The truth in the first verse is the source from which the rest of the message in the Scriptures comes. In the same way, the Torah is the foundation upon which all other truths are built. The first book is called Beresheet—the Beginning. It contains, in seed form, the beginning of all the truths found in the Scriptures.

Noach.title: The Days of Noah and the Last Days

blocks.t: “As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” (Mt 24:37)

Because the time of the coming of the Messiah will be like the days of Noah, it is important to study the time before the flood to gain understanding. Paul also wrote, “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.” (Rom 15:4)

It says in the book of Hebrews that Noah obeyed God “concerning events as yet unseen.” This required faith or trust. Through his trust, he condemned the world, since they did not believe what God had said. According to Jewish tradition, Noah worked on building the ark for 120 years from the day that God said, “My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years.” (Gen 6:3) When God pronounced this judgment, He also began to prepare a way of escape. Noah was the only one who listened. He began to build the ark.
Peter wrote about this,

“…knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, ‘Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.’ For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.” (2 Pet 3:3–7)

The first world was deluged with water and perished. This was truly an event yet unseen. Nothing like it had ever happened before. In the same way, God’s promised judgment of the world through fire has never happened before, in the history of mankind. Just like the people around Noah made fun of him when he built on the ark, people today also make fun of “fundamentalists” who talk about God’s judgment and the soon coming of Messiah.

Yeshua said, “For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” (Mt 24:38–39) In the days of Noah, the people had no idea what was about to happen to them, despite the fact that Noah had been building on the ark for 120 years. It will be the same in the last days. The question is: do we today believe just as strongly in a day of judgment by fire that will soon come, as Noah believed in a day of judgment through a flood in his day? Are we preparing for this? Peter continued to write:

“Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.” (2 Pet 3:11–14)

Peter wrote that those who say that all things are continuing as they have been from the beginning of creation are overlooking the flood. Nature confirms the flood of Noah through all the fossils. Dead animals normally do not produce any fossils. The flood of Noah, however, which in an instant buried the animals under the colossal weight of the landmasses covering them, gives an explanation for all the fossils. Nature proves the accuracy of Scripture and God’s righteous judgment, leaving mankind without any excuse.
Please notice that even if the world that existed before Noah “perished” it did not mean that the whole planet ceased to exist. Peter wrote about the present world:

“But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.” (2 Pet 3:10)

Some translations say: “both the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.” (NKJV) This is misleading because the rest of Scripture shows us that the present planet will not cease to exist. It will rather be renewed similar to what happens when a field is burnt with fire. Everything visible is consumed, but after the fire, new life springs up.

Vayigash.title: Joseph Makes Himself Known

blocks.t: “So no one stayed with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers. And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it.” (Gen 45:1–2)
What a moment it will be, when Yeshua of Nazareth reveals Himself in the end times, in Jerusalem, to His own brothers, as Messiah ben Yoseph! The tears will flow freely.

“And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child, and weep bitterly over him, as one weeps over a firstborn. On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. The land shall mourn, each family by itself.” (Zec 12:10–12)

Yeshua has wept over His people, now, for almost two thousand years. He has longed for them—just as Joseph did. It also says about Joseph: “He cried, ‘Make everyone go out from me.’” (Gen 45:1) Paul wrote about the return of Messiah to Jerusalem: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God.” (1 Th 4:16)

“And Joseph said to his brothers, ‘I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?’” (v. 3) Joseph’s first question concerned his father. Despite his exaltation and success in Egypt, he had not forgotten Jacob. He had longed for him, all this time. In the same way, Yeshua belongs among the descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, even though they have rejected Him, while the Gentiles have accepted Him and made Him the leader of the largest religion in world history.

“But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence. So Joseph said to his brothers, ‘Come near to me, please.’ And they came near. And he said, ‘I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.’” (v. 3–4)

The brothers could not understand how the Egyptian ruler Zaphenath-paneah, standing before them, could be their own brother Joseph. They were dumbfounded. The NIV translation says that, “they were terrified at his presence.” Joseph asked them to come closer to him. “And they came near. And he said, ‘I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.’” (v. 4) Why did Joseph tell his brothers to come to him? According to Rashi, Joseph showed the brothers that he was circumcised. He showed them the sign of the covenant, so that they would understand that he was their brother.
Also, Joseph told them that they had sold him as a slave to Egypt. No one besides Joseph and the brothers would have known about this.

Further down in the text, it says, “And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you.” (v. 12) The brothers did not only see that Joseph was circumcised. The expression “my mouth” means that Joseph spoke to them in Hebrew without the need of any interpreter.

Joseph was quick to tell them that they should not grieve about what they had done to him. Now that they had repented of their envy and selfishness, what they had done was no longer a problem. On the contrary—it was part of God’s plan to save them! In the same way, Messiah’s death on the cross has brought life to the whole world—including to His own people.

“And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For the famine has been in the land these two years, and there are yet five years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. And God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth, and to keep alive for you many survivors. So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.” (v. 5–8)

Both verses 5 and 8 begin with the same expression in Hebrew, which means: “And now…” Joseph wanted to emphasize that a new time had now come. He wanted them to forget about the past and put it behind them! “And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here… And now, it was not you who sent me here, but God.” Indeed a new time will begin when the Messiah is reconciled with His own brothers in Jerusalem. “For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?” (Ro 11:15)

“Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck. And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. After that his brothers talked with him.” (v. 14–15) It is important to be able to weep. Tears are healing. God has created us with the ability to weep. It proves that our hearts are not hard.
The Haftarah text from the prophets for the Torah portion Vayigash is Ezekiel 37:15–28, which deals with the uniting of Judah and Ephraim into one, in the LORD’s hand.

“The word of the LORD came to me: ‘Son of man, take a stick and write on it, ‘For Judah, and the people of Israel associated with him’; then take another stick and write on it, ‘For Joseph (the stick of Ephraim) and all the house of Israel associated with him.’ And join them one to another into one stick, that they may become one in your hand. And when your people say to you, ‘Will you not tell us what you mean by these?’ tell them, Thus says the Lord GOD: ‘Behold, I am about to take the stick of Joseph (that is in the hand of Ephraim) and the tribes of Israel associated with him. And I will join with it the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, that they may be one in my hand. …My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd.’”

Ephraim is, as we have mentioned before, a picture of the disciples of Messiah ben Joseph, Yeshua of Nazareth, among the Gentiles. Even though there is a literal fulfillment of this prophecy, where the ten “lost tribes” are reunited with Judah, the prophecy in Ezekiel is also referring to the uniting of Jew and Gentile in Messiah.

God’s plan of salvation for the world runs along the two “tracks” of Joseph and Judah. Joseph and Ephraim represent Messiah and his disciples in the end times, and Judah represents the physical descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, with the covenants and the promises. When Ephraim and Judah are united into one, they combine to make a double, or twofold, river of life. The uniting of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt is, therefore, also a prophecy about this life-changing uniting of all of Israel.

“To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes. To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey. Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, ‘Do not quarrel on the way.’” (v. 22–24)

When Benjamin was caught with Joseph’s silver cup, all the brothers tore their clothes. Now, Joseph gave them new sets of clothing. These were no ordinary clothes, but festive garments befitting close relatives of the ruler in Egypt. A new life had begun. Benjamin got five new sets of festive garments and 300 shekels of silver. It was within Benjamin’s territory that the Temple, with the altar bringing atonement (the silver), would later be situated, and where five of the annual Feasts would be celebrated before the LORD: Passover, including the Feast of Unleavened Bread and First fruits, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tabernacles. (See Dt 16:16)

The last thing that Joseph told the brothers was not to quarrel on the way back. He did not want them to argue over who was most at fault for betraying him. All of them were forgiven, and this was now in the past.

Vayigash.book: Messiah in the Torah, Vol. I

Vayechi.title: Jacob Lives

blocks.t: “And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years.” (Gen 47:28)

And so we have arrived at the final Torah portion in Genesis and the conclusion of Jacob’s toldot, i.e. “the generations of Jacob” (Gen 37:2). This portion is called VaYechi and it means, “He lived”. This is a prophetic title. Jacob lived on, in Egypt. Israel is the people of the future. In a well-known, popular Hebrew song, we sing “Am Yisrael Chai,” meaning “The people of Israel live.” Israel is the eternal nation that God has promised to watch over until the end of time. Yeshua said, “Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” (Mt 24:34)

The final verse of the previous section reads, “Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.” (Gen 47:27) By this time, Jacob’s descendants had become numerous. In the beginning, they were very successful—both materially and in numbers. They acquired possessions and multiplied greatly; their numerical increase was, in fact, supernatural, but they lived in a strange land.

The book of Genesis begins with the Messiah (Gen 1:1), the Sabbath (Gen 2:1–3), and the Garden of Eden (Gen 2:8). It ends with the chosen people finding themselves in Egypt, in the house of slavery. This shows us that everyone, even the people who are God’s own special possession, are in need of salvation through the Messiah. “…for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Messiah Yeshua” (Ro 3:23–24). We will study this great and glorious salvation in greater detail later on, in Exodus.

The portion VaYechi is unique in the sense that it is the only Torah portion in the handwritten Torah scrolls where there is no space at all between the end of the previous portion (VaYigash) and the beginning of this portion (VaYechi). Rashi interprets this to mean that VaYechi is a “hidden Torah portion,” in the spiritual sense, as well. The children of Israel were not aware of the fact that they were stuck in Egypt and that it would result in slavery. One Jewish Midrash interprets the verse “And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly” to mean that Egypt “grasped” the children of Israel but it was hidden from them. It is this way for all people. Before salvation, we are unaware of the fact that we are lost and enslaved to sin.

In this week’s Torah portion, one of the greatest mysteries in the Scriptures is also presented—the grafting of Gentile believers into Israel through faith in Messiah ben Joseph. Paul wrote about this as a mystery that has been hidden. “When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Messiah, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.” (Eph 3:4–5) After the Apostles, this mystery eventually once again disappeared in the Church. It is now being revealed again in these days. (We will discuss more about this, later on in this commentary.)
